list.listitem: PCOS is a clinical diagnosis based on the presence of 2 of the following 3 criteria: (1) oligomenorrhea or anovulation, (2) clinical and/or biochemical evidence of hyperandrogenism, and (3) polycystic ovaries on ultrasound. C
Adolescents require stricter criteria for accurate diagnosis. C

Diagnosis requires exclusion of other related disorders and work-up should include prolactin, TSH, morning 17-OHP (if clinically indicated), and total testosterone, with or without DHEA-S. In women with a confirmed diagnoses, screening for metabolic syndrome is recommended. C
Combination low-dose oral contraceptives (OCs) can be used to regulate menstrual cycles and decrease hirsutism. B

Only clomiphene and letrozole improve live birth rates and are considered first line therapy for infertility related to PCOS. Letrozole is more effective than clomiphene based on a recent meta-analysis. A Metformin alone does not improve live birth rates, but may be helpful when combined with other fertility agents. A
Weight loss of as little as 5% can improve regular menses and improve response to ovulation inducing and fertility medications. A

background.definition: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a clinical diagnosis characterized by menstrual irregularity, clinical or laboratory evidence of elevated androgens, and polycystic ovarian morphology (POM).

list.listitem: One in 10 women of reproductive age are affected with PCOS, with an overall prevalence of 6% to 10% based on the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) criteria.
Using the Rotterdam criteria which includes a broader definition, the prevalence is as high as 15%.
Health care cost associated with diagnosis and treatment is estimated at more than $4 billion annually in the United States.
Individuals with PCOS have approximately a 4-fold increase in type 2 diabetes mellitus and a 2- to 3-fold increased risk of metabolic syndrome.

High quality studies demonstrate an association between metabolic syndrome and PCOS, both in those with and without obesity.One study showed that adolescents diagnosed with PCOS have a higher prevalence of metabolic syndrome, 10.8% in adolescents with PCOS compared with 1.7% in those without PCOS.

There is evidence of increased prevalence of psychological disorders (depression and anxiety) in women with PCOS. Women with PCOS appear to have increased odds of having an eating disorder diagnosis (OR 3.87, 95% CI 1.43-10.49; four studies).
The cause of PCOS is likely multifactorial. Excess androgen production, likely secondary to insulin resistance, plays a major role in the disease process.
Genetic predisposition is likely based on small family, receptor gene polymorphism, and genome-wide association studies.
Aberrant expression of several micro RNAs also appears to play a role in pathogenesis of PCOS.
Both interleukin-6 rs1800795 polymorphism and vascular endothelial growth factor gene polymorphisms appear to be protective against PCOS susceptibility.

Authors of a cross-trait analysis found positive genetic correlations between PCOS and adult and childhood body mass index (BMI, rg 0.47 and 0.31, respectively) and waist-to-hip ratio suggesting a shared genetic basis underlying obesity and PCOS.
One study found a link between PCOS and blood levels of an industrial compound (bisphenol A) used in the synthesis of polycarbonate plastics; this compound acts as an endocrine disrupter.
Insulin resistance is believed to play an intrinsic role in PCOS by disrupting the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis causing ovulatory dysfunction.

Elevated insulin levels lead to increased androgen production from ovarian theca cells and decreased liver synthesis of sex hormone-binding globulin, resulting in higher levels of biologically active "free" testosterone.
Increased gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) pulsatility results in higher luteinizing hormone (LH) to follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) ratios favoring ovarian testosterone production.
Vascular endothelial growth factor appears to have a role in the pathophysiology of PCOS as a mediator of ovarian hyperstimulation.
Abnormal retinoid signaling and abnormal anti-Müllerian hormone-mediated signaling may also be involved in the pathogenesis of PCOS.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Use of gonadotropin releasing hormone analog for early puberty
Use of valproate vs. other drugs for women with epilepsy

list.listitem: Suspect PCOS in adults with oligomenorrhea or anovulation, clinical and/or laboratory evidence of hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound. C
Diagnosis requires exclusion of other related disorders and work-up should include prolactin, TSH, morning 17-OHP, and total testosterone, with or without DHEA-S. C
Measurement of gonadotropins and/or insulin levels is not required. C
Stricter criteria are necessary to confirm the diagnosis of PCOS in adolescents. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Irregular menstrual cycles associated with galactorrhea; elevated prolactin
Irregular menstrual cycles with minimal hyperandrogenism; elevated TSH
Screen all patients with suspected PCOS; most common in Ashkenazi Jews; morning 17-OHP
Associated hypertension, abdominal striae, easy bruising; elevated 24-hour urine cortisol
Rapid virilization; initiate evaluation if total serum testosterone levels >200 ng/dL
Acral enlargement, coarse features, prognathism; elevated insulin-like growth factor I (ILG-I)

list.listitem: Rotterdam 2003 diagnostic criteria include 2 of the following 3 features: (1) oligomenorrhea and/or anovulation, (2) clinical and/or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism, and (3) polycystic ovarian morphology (PCOM).
NIH 1990 diagnostic criteria include both: (a) hyperandrogenism and/or hyperandrogenemia and (b) chronic oligomenorrhea/anovulation.
Diagnosis per the AE-PCOS 2009 criteria must include hyperandrogenism (either clinical or laboratory) plus one of the following: either (a) polycystic ovaries OR (b) oligomenorrhea/anovulation.

Diagnosis in adolescents should include: oligomenorrhea for >2 years or primary amenorrhea after age 16 years, hyperandrogenemia (rather than just clinical signs of androgen excess), and presence of polycystic ovaries with ovarian size >10 cm3.

Amenorrhea/oligomenorrhea and hirsutism are the most common presenting symptoms and are sufficient to make the diagnosis. Hirsutism is defined as excess terminal hair in a male-type pattern, most frequently on the upper lip, chin, periareolar area and the linea alba.

While alopecia and adult acne are commonly reported symptoms in PCOS, they are not consistently associated with hyperandrogenemia and therefore should not be used as a clinical sign of androgen excess in diagnosis.
The prevalence of symptoms in persons with PCOS is summarized in Table 1.
Family history of PCOS increases patient risk for development of the disorder.
Careful review of medications may identify those with androgenic side-effects, such as danazol, steroids, and anticonvulsants.

While PCOS may be diagnosed based solely on clinical criteria (anovulation/oligomenorrhea and cutaneous signs of hyperandrogenism), laboratory testing is necessary to exclude other diagnoses and helps to confirm clinical diagnosis for PCOS.

Many guidelines recommend TSH, urine pregnancy test, prolactin and 17-hydroxyprogesterone to exclude thyroid disease, pregnancy, prolactinoma, and nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia, respectively. Testing for other possible causes (see Differential Diagnosis section) is based on clinical suspicion.
Measurements of insulin resistance, including fasting glucose and fasting insulin ratios, have failed to consistently differentiate patients with PCOS.

Although LH and the LH:FSH ratio demonstrate high likelihood ratios for PCOS, they are not included in the diagnostic criteria because values are influenced by the temporal relationship to ovulation, body mass index (value is higher in lean women with PCOS), and by the assay system used.

Total testosterone and DHEA-S tests establish laboratory evidence of androgen excess in cases where clinical signs of hyperandrogenism are absent. However, normal testosterone or DHEA levels do not rule out PCOS (sensitivity 42%-50%). Use of free testosterone assays in adolescents is problematic due to limited sensitivity. Extremely high testosterone values are indicative of a possible ovarian or adrenal neoplasm (see Differential Diagnosis section) .

Anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) testing has been proposed as a possible alternative to ultrasound for identifying PCOM. Authors of a meta-analysis of 29 studies found a pooled sensitivity and specificity for AMH alone in detecting PCOS of 76% and 86% (LR+ 5.4, LR- 0.28), respectively, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.88 (95% CI 0.85-0.91). The AUC improved to 0.97 (95% CI 0.95-0.98) when AMH was substituted for PCOM. However, the true utility of AMH testing in PCOS diagnosis continues to be investigated. A 2021 long-term follow up study using data from a large prospective cohort in the Netherlands demonstrated that AMH testing in adolescence was not a useful prognostic indicator for PCOS in adulthood. A 2019 systematic review studying the diagnostic utility of AMH testing in PCOS identified several limitations, including variability in assays used, inconsistent definitions of PCOM for adequate comparison and disparate threshold values.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 11 studies found that elevated serum ferritin was strongly associated with PCOS, with values for serum ferritin showing good potential in discriminating patients with and without PCOS (AUC = 0.827).

Transvaginal ultrasound is only used to confirm diagnosis in cases where only one criterion is present, either menstrual irregularity or signs of androgen excess (clinical or biochemical). Conversely, a polycystic appearance of the ovaries is seen in up to one third of women and does not imply PCOS or subfertility.

In a reproductive-aged adults, two of the following three criteria are required to make the diagnosis: (1) infertility, oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea; (2) hirsutism, acanthosis nigricans, or laboratory evidence of androgen excess; (3) polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound.

Use laboratory testing to rule out secondary causes of hyperandrogenism (see Differential Diagnosis section) and/or to establish evidence of elevated androgens when clinical signs are absent. At a minimum, obtain prolactin, TSH, morning 17-OHP, total serum testosterone, with or without DHEA-S.

Only order a pelvic ultrasound to assess PCOM in adults meeting only one diagnostic criteria for PCOS, either ovulatory dysfunction or hyperandrogenism. Ultrasound may also be useful for adolescents with suspected PCOS.
Once the diagnosis of PCOS is confirmed, screen for glucose intolerance and dyslipidemia.
Obtain an endometrial biopsy or ultrasound in patients with prolonged amenorrhea or abnormal uterine bleeding to rule out malignancy.

list.listitem: Combination OCs can be effective treatments for regulating menstrual cycles and decreasing hirsutism. A
Medical therapy for at least 6 months is necessary to determine the effectiveness for treating hirsutism. C
Antiandrogens are effective therapy for hirsutism. A
Spironolactone is a useful adjunct for the treatment of hirsutism but cannot be used during pregnancy. B

Clomiphene and letrozole are first-line therapy for infertility; letrozole is more effective than clomiphene based on a recent meta-analysis. A When combined with clomiphene, metformin may increase pregnancy rates in obese women with PCOS. A
There is insufficient evidence to treat insulin resistance in the absence of glucose intolerance or type 2 diabetes. C
Drug treatment(s) should target specific symptoms and treatment goals of the patient which can include manifestations of androgen excess and ovulatory dysfunction.
Current evidence does not support pharmacologic treatment of insulin resistance in patients with PCOS in the absence of impaired glucose tolerance.

Many studies on pharmacologic treatments for PCOS focus on disease-oriented outcomes such as biochemical parameters rather than patient-oriented outcomes. A 2021 systematic review showed improvement in total cholesterol, triglyceride, LDL, testosterone, and fasting insulin level with metformin (varying regimens) combined with simvastatin (20 mg QD) as compared to metformin alone. Another systematic review found that atorvastatin 20 or 40 mg QD can lower fasting insulin & HOMA-IR but may not have an effect on fasting glucose level or BMI; patient-oriented outcomes were not examined.

listitem.strong: Treatment of symptoms, including menstrual irregularity and hirsutism

list.listitem: Low-dose combination OCs are effective treatments for hirsutism and acne and also regulate menses to protect against endometrial hyperplasia. Combination OCs are not associated with clinically significant adverse metabolic consequences.
Cyclic progestins every 1 to 3 months should be considered in patients who cannot take OCs and are anovulatory to protect against endometrial cancer.

Metformin can be used to help with menstrual irregularity, either alone or with combination OCs in both adults and adolescents with PCOS. In a cohort study of 119 women with PCOS at a single institution, use of metformin over 24 months resulted in increased menstrual frequency and other disease-oriented outcomes such as decreased BMI, testosterone, and LH levels, most within the first 6 month of treatment.
Low-quality evidence suggests that GLP-1 receptor agonists do not further improve menstrual frequency when compared to or when used with metformin.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 10 small RCTs found increased frequency of menstrual cycles (RR 6.8, 95% CI 2.8-16.6) with the carbocyclic sugar, inositol, when compared to placebo. Single trials demonstrated ignificantly improved ovulation rates (RR 2.3, 95% CI 1.1-4.7) and, compared to placebo or metformin.

Antiandrogens such as spironolactone (100-200 mg daily), flutamide (125-250 mg daily to twice daily) and finasteride (2.5-5 mg daily) have been shown to be equally effective for treating hirsutism. Teratogenic potential of these medications should be discussed when clinically applicable.

In a recent RCT of 70 women with PCOS, those receiving combination OCs and the anti-androgen, bicalutamide, for 12 months had a greater reduction in hirsutism as measured by videodermoscopy than those on combination OCs plus placebo; both treatments, however, were effective in reducing hirsutism. The only adverse effect reported for the anti-androgen treatment was an increase in total cholesterol and low-density lipoprotein.

Authors of a Cochrane review of pharmacologic therapies for hirsutism in women of reproductive age found low quality evidence supporting OCs, flutamide 250 mg twice daily, and spironolactone 100 mg daily. The authors found inconsistent results for finasteride and GnRH analogues and no effect on hirsutism from metformin use or hypocaloric diets.
There is insufficient evidence to recommend pharmacologic management of obesity in PCOS as a first line treatment.
One meta-analysis found that thiazolidinediones are inferior to metformin monotherapy for reducing BMI.

Metformin treatment alone or in combination with an OC was associated with weight loss compared with OC use alone in one RCT of 90 women with PCOS (−3.0 [−10.3; 0.6], −1.9 [−4.9; 0.1], and 1.2 [−0.8; 3.0] kg, respectively) at 1 year.

AACE (2015), ACOG (2018) and ASRM (2018) recommend clomiphene citrate or letrozole for treatment of anovulatory infertility in women with PCOS. Clomiphene citrate increases FSH and LH thereby stimulating the growth of the ovarian follicle. Letrozole, a non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor, lowers estrogen production.

In a double-blinded multicenter 1:1 trial, where 750 women with PCOS were randomized to either letrozole or clomiphene arms, study authors found letrozole used for up to 5 cycles resulted in more cumulative live births than clomiphene (27.5% vs. 19.1%, P = 0.007). More congenital anomalies occurred in the letrozole group than the clomiphene group, but this was not statistically significant. There was a higher incidence of hot flushes among women on clomiphene and a higher incidence of fatigue and dizziness among women on letrozole.

Authors of a systematic review and network meta-analysis of treatment for women with WHO group II anovulation (i.e., dysfunctions of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis) found that both letrozole and combination clomiphene/metformin were associated with higher ovulation rates (OR 1.99, 95% CI 1.38-2.87 and 1.55, 95% CI 1.02-2.36; respectively) and higher pregnancy rates (OR 1.58, 95% CI 1.25-2.00 and 1.81, 95% CI 1.35-2.42; respectively). Letrozole led to 1.5-fold higher live birth rates than clomiphene alone, and both letrozole and metformin were associated with a lower multiple rate than clomiphene.

In the most recent meta-analysis, authors concluded that letrozole was more effective than clomiphene for all primary outcomes, with a higher pregnancy rate (28 studies with 3936 participants; 35% vs 23%; RR 1.48, 1.34 - 1.63), and live birth rate (8 studies with 1725 participants; 33% vs 22%; RR 1.49, 1.27 - 1.74) based on moderate certainty of evidence.

Data regarding the efficacy of metformin, either alone or in combination with another fertility-inducing agent, remain mixed. One large prospective trial of 320 women found that metformin with standard fertility treatment increased live birth rates compared to placebo (41.9% vs. 28.8%, P = 0.014).

In an updated Cochrane review of insulin-sensitizing drugs, authors found that metformin used alone may be beneficial over placebo for live birth, although quality of evidence was low. Results were inconclusive when metformin was compared to clomiphene; however, among obese women, clinical pregnancy and ovulation suggests that clomiphene is preferable to metformin for ovulation induction. Combination metformin plus clomiphene improves clinical pregnancy rates over clomiphene alone, but it is not clear if this results in improved live birth rate.

The ASRM (2018) guideline states that metformin should not be used as first-line therapy for ovulation induction as it is less effective than other agents and that there was insufficient evidence that metformin in combination with other agents used to induce ovulation increases live-birth rates.

In a double-blind clinical trial, 626 participants were randomized into three groups: clomiphene/placebo, metformin/placebo and clomiphene/metformin. There was a significantly lower live birth rate in the metformin/placebo group than in the clomiphene/placebo group and the combination-therapy group (P < 0.001 for both comparisons). Similarly, authors of a 2014 Cochrane review found no conclusive evidence from 9 RCTs that metformin treatment before or during ART cycles improved live birth rates.
Although there is limited evidence to support gonadotropin therapy for PCOS, ACOG recommends a low-dose regimen of gonadotropin as second-line therapy if pregnancy fails to result from clomiphene.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 15 trials with 2387 women, 10 of which compared recombinant FSH with urinary-derived gonadotrophins, concluded that there was little or no difference in live birth, incidence of multiple pregnancy, clinical pregnancy rate, or miscarriage rate between these treatments in women with PCOS.

In an RCT of 96 clomiphene-resistant patients with PCOS, there was no significant difference between letrozole and human menopausal gonadotropin in number of ovulation cycles (53.6% vs. 64.7%), clinical pregnancy rates (22.9% vs. 27.1%) or abortion rates (6.2% vs. 10.4%).

Metformin may have a role in women at increased risk for ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) who undergo gonadotropin-stimulated in vitro fertilization. A recent study found a 28% relative reduction in OHSS in those treated with 500 mg of metformin three times daily.
Laparoscopic ovarian drilling (LOD) using electrocautery or laser can be used for controlled ovarian stromal destruction resulting in decreased serum androgens and ovulation induction.
ACOG considers LOD a second-line therapy noting that the fertility benefits may be temporary and long-term effects are unclear.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 38 trials including 3326 women with PCOS who failed clomiphene treatment found LOD may slightly decrease live birth rates when compared to medical ovulation induction alone (28%-40% vs. 42%, respectively); this difference was not observed when only the four studies at low risk of bias were included. Medications included clomiphene citrate+tamoxifen, gonadotrophins, or aromatase inhibitors. However, rates of multiple pregnancy are likely lower for women who conceive after LOD compared to gonadotrophins (OR 0.34; 95% CI 0.18-0.66).
In another meta-analysis, LOD was comparable to letrozole for achieving live births in patients with clomiphene-resistant PCOS.

Authors of a Cochrane review found insufficient high-quality evidence to support the use of acupuncture for menstrual frequency, ovulation or clinical pregnancy in women with PCOS. In an RCT of Chinese women with PCOS and infertility, active acupuncture treatment plus clomiphene provided no additional benefit over sham acupuncture treatment plus clomiphene for increasing live birth rate.

However, in a more recent meta-analysis of 22 studies with 2315 patients, acupuncture was helpful for recovery of menses based on 5 trials but there were no significant differences in the live birth, pregnancy, and ovulation rates based on limited evidence.
A Maitake mushroom extract may be useful alone or as an adjunct with clomiphene in inducing ovulation.
Cinnamon supplementation of 1.5 g/d improved menstrual cycles in one small RCT. Pooling data from five clinical trials, cinnamon had a positive effect on lipid parameters.

Cochrane authors found insufficient evidence to support the use of Chinese herbal medicine (CHM) for women with PCOS and subfertility, although there is low-quality evidence supporting use of combined CHM and clomiphene to improve pregnancy rates.

Authors of a metanalysis of RCTs and quasi-RCTs of Chinese herbal medicine combined with moxibustion found support for use of this combination with or without clomiphene to increase pregnancy rates in infertile women compared to Western medicine alone (RR for pregnancy rate as an adjunct was 1.65 (95% CI 1.29-2.11). 30412108 Data quality was poor.
Cosmetic treatments such as electrolysis and laser treatment for permanent hair removal are effective.
Topical eflornithine 13.9% (Vaniqa) slows facial hair growth with continued use. The addition of eflornithine to laser treatment is superior to laser treatment alone.
Topical minoxidil can improve male-pattern baldness.
Weight loss, exercise and lifestyle change is helpful for restoring ovulation and achieving pregnancy in overweight women with PCOS.

Modest weight loss of 5% to 7% improves ovulatory function and reduces insulin resistance resulting in lower serum androgen levels in patients with a body mass index of greater than 30. Weight loss also improves associated metabolic abnormalities, including insulin resistance. Specific low-carbohydrate/high protein diets are no more effective in improving menstrual cyclicity or insulin resistance than other types of calorie restriction.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 10 RCTs on exercise confirmed that aerobic exercise alone was beneficial for reducing BMI in women with PCOS based on moderate evidence but limited evidence to discern an effect of exercise on reproductive function.

Authors of a Cochrane review of lifestyle interventions confirm positive effects of lifestyle interventions on reduced weight and hyperandrogenism (free androgen index) in women with PCOS, based on low-quality evidence.

In a recent three-armed RCT, women randomized preconception to lifestyle intervention or lifestyle plus OCs lost more weight (mean loss about −6%) and had superior cumulative ovulation rates (60% and 67% vs. 46%) compared to women on OCs alone.
Authors of another meta-analysis found no differences between lifestyle interventions and metformin with respect to improvements in menstrual cycles, pregnancy rates and BMI.

Authors of a systematic review of diet and PCOS found that weight loss improved the presentation of PCOS regardless of dietary composition. Subtle differences between diets included greater weight loss for a monounsaturated fat-enriched diet, improved depression and self-esteem for a high-protein diet, improved menstrual regularity and quality of life for a low-glycemic index diet, and greater reductions in insulin resistance, fibrinogen, total, and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol for a low-carbohydrate or low-glycemic index diet.
Fertility appears lower when both partners smoke, so smoking cessation should be recommended for such couples.
Early referral for treatment of infertility is important since metformin alone has inferior pregnancy outcomes compared with hormonal treatment.
The Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada recommend expert advice about pregnancy risk for women who are morbidly obese with PCOS.

Patients have persistent symptoms until menopause when abnormal ovarian androgen production decreases. C However, women with PCOS continue to have elevated serum androgen levels even after menopause compared to control women, although the difference narrows.

PCOS is associated with many cardiovascular risk factors such as diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and obesity. B Authors of a meta-analysis of 16 studies, including 12 that were population-based, found a pooled HR for CV events (e.g., coronary arterial disease myocardial infarction, angina, heart failure, and ischemic heart disease) in reproductive-aged patients with PCOS of 1.38 (95% CI 1.12-1.71) and in menopausal/aging patients with PCOS of 1.53 (95% CI 1.15, 2.04) compared to healthy controls.

There is also evidence of increased an approximately 1.5-fold increased risk of hypertension in reproductive-age patients with PCOS but this was not true for menopausal/aging patients who had PCOS during their reproductive years.

Authors conducting a secondary analysis of the Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP) and the Diabetes Prevention Program Outcomes Study (DPPOS) found no increased risk of diabetes or coronary artery disease among enrolled midlife women who were already glucose intolerant and overweight based on the presence of irregular menses or increased androgen concentrations as measured by free androgen index.
Impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) and type 2 diabetes (T2DM) are more prevalent (OR 4:1) in those with PCOS, with approximately 40% of women becoming affected by age 50 years. C
Rates of progression from normal to impaired glucose tolerance in women with PCOS may be as high as 5% to 15% within 3 years.
Women with PCOS have a 2.7-fold increased risk for endometrial cancer, but are not at increased risk for ovarian or breast cancer. B

Screening for glucose intolerance and type 2 diabetes is recommended. Hemoglobin A1C has poor sensitivity (35%) for diagnosing diabetes. AACE recommends consideration of an oral glucose tolerance test every 1 to 2 years based on family history of T2DM as well as body mass index (BMI) and yearly in women with IGT.
A fasting lipid profile can be useful in identifying associated dyslipidemias.
AACE recommends that women considering pregnancy should be screened and treated for hypertension and diabetes prior to attempting conception.

Patients with PCOS who successfully become pregnant have an increased risk of gestational diabetes (40%-50%), pregnancy-induced hypertension, preeclampsia (5%), preterm birth, and small for gestational-age babies (10%-15%). If GDM is present, macrosomia may occur. In addition to these pregnancy complications, authors of a meta-analysis also found higher rates of cesarean delivery, hypoglycemia and perinatal death.
A higher risk of preterm delivery in twin pregnancies among patients with PCOS has also been reported (51% vs. 43%; RR 1.18; 95% CI 1.03-1.37).
These increased risks appear to be independent of obesity, but associated with hyperandrogenic PCOS phenotypes.

For patients with PCOS who become pregnancy following in-vitro fertilization, authors of a meta-analysis of 29 studies found an approximately 1.5-fold higher risk of miscarriage, 5-fold risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, 2.5-fold risk of gestational diabetes mellitus, 2-fold risk of pregnancy-induced hypertension, 1.6-fold risk of preterm birth and 2-fold increased risk for large-for-gestational-age babies compared to those with other causes of infertility who had undergone IVF.
Babies born to women with PCOS have an increase likelihood of admission to a neonatal intensive care unit (OR 2.31) and perinatal mortality (OR 3.07).

In an Australian database study, offspring of women with PCOS were at higher risk compared to offspring of women without PCOS of preterm birth (15.5% vs. 7.6%); perinatal mortality (2.3% vs. 0.7%); more postnatal hospitalizations (14.1% vs. 7.9%) and later hospitalizations for conditions including metabolic disorder, disease of the nervous system and asthma; and more congenital anomalies (6.3% vs. 4.9%), cardiovascular defects (1.5% vs. 1.0%), and urogenital defects (2.0% vs. 1.4%).
PCOS was associated with an approximately 1.6-fold increase in autism spectrum disorder in their offspring based on a meta-analysis of 7 studies.

listitem.strong: Metformin use during pregnancy – potential benefits and risks

list.listitem: Authors of a meta-analysis of 6 studies, including 3 RCTs, found metformin reduced the proportion of patients developing gestational diabetes (log OR -1.27, 95% CI -2.24 to -0.30). This is in contrast to two RCTs that did not find benefit from metformin use during pregnancy on gestational diabetes.

Authors of another meta-analysis of 5 RCTs and 8 cohort studies found that metformin treatment during pregnancy reduced rates of early pregnancy loss and prevalence of preterm delivery (OR 0.37; 95% CI 0.20-0.68).

Metformin use during pregnancy, however, may result in adverse effects on exposed infants and children. Based on an RCT of women with PCOS and their 258 offspring, metformin-exposed infants of obese women had larger heads at birth (head circumference 35.6 cm versus 35.1 cm for non-exposed infants). Metformin-exposed infants of non-obese women had reduced length and reduced weight compared to non-exposed infants and reduced length compared to a reference population.

In one follow-up study of 182 children of mothers with PCOS who participated in two RCTs of metformin 1700 or 2000 mg/d vs. placebo from first trimester to delivery, metformin-exposed children at age 4 years had higher BMI z scores and there were more overweight/obese children compared to children who were not exposed (26 [32%] vs. 14 [18%]). Increased BMI in children exposed to metformin vs. placebo during pregnancy was also reported in a 5-10-year follow-up of an RCT (difference in means 0.41, 95% CI 0.03-0.78), although only 55% of exposed children participated.

Among 131 women (55% of those initially enrolled) who participated in a RCT of metformin use during pregnancy, there were no differences between exposed and non-exposed women at 7.7 years follow-up in BMI, waist/hip ratio, blood pressure, lipids, glucose and insulin levels, or prevalence of metabolic syndrome.
Consensus on diagnosing PCOS in adolescence has not been reached.

The diagnosis of PCOS is difficult in this age group because 40% of adolescents have polycystic ovaries on ultrasound, anovulation is present in more than half of teenagers at 3 years post-menarche, and acne is common.

Formal diagnosis should be attempted in adolescent girls presenting with hirsutism or menstrual irregularities since PCOS is associated with not only the long-term health consequences of insulin resistance but also with poor self-esteem.

The PCOS consensus workshop group cautions against over-diagnosis and recommends that all three of the Rotterdam criteria be present to make a diagnosis of PCOS; this stricter criteria should include: oligomenorrhea for >2 years or primary amenorrhea after age 16 years, hyperandrogenemia (rather than just clinical signs of androgen excess), and presence of polycystic ovaries with ovarian size >10 cm3.
Adolescents should be treated primarily with diet and exercise. OCs are useful for regulating menses, as well as for improving symptoms of acne and hirsutism.
Evidence for treatment of ovulatory dysfunction and metabolic complications with metformin is limited in this age group; metformin may help with weight loss.
